dumbbell-step-up.name: Dumbbell Step-Up
dumbbell-step-up.execution: Face a box or bench (30-50cm). Place one foot fully on top. Drive through the box foot — extend hip and knee to stand fully on top. Bring the trailing foot up. Stand tall — full hip extension at the top. Step back down with control. The driving leg stays on the box. Complete all reps one side before switching. Add dumbbells at sides as bodyweight becomes easy.
dumbbell-step-up.why: The step-up is the foundational single-leg vertical strength exercise — building the glute, quad, and hip control needed for powerful skating push-offs. Because one leg is working while the other only supports, it identifies and corrects bilateral strength deficits that compound over a career of dominant-side skating. A basic but essential movement that should be in every hockey player's program at some point.
dumbbell-step-up.transfer: Single-leg strength in the exact pattern of skating stride. Three sets × 8 per leg, controlled tempo. Heavy enough that the last rep is honest.
dumbbell-step-up.cues: "Full foot on box" · "Drive through heel" · "Stand tall at top" · "Lower with control"
dumbbell-step-up.mistakes: Pushing off the floor foot — all drive from the box leg only. Knee caving inward — push it out over the toes. Not reaching full hip extension at the top — stand TALL on each rep. Box too low — at or above knee height for real demand.
dumbbell-step-up.progression: Progress: Lateral step-up then crossover step-up — progress through the variations. | Regress: Low step (20cm) step-up — build confidence and stability before raising the height.

lateral-step-up.name: Lateral Step-Up
lateral-step-up.execution: Stand beside a box (30-50cm), side-on. Place the near foot fully on the top of the box. Drive through the box foot — extend hip and knee — to stand on top. Bring the trailing foot up to meet the top foot. Stand tall. Step back down with control. The driving leg stays on the box. Complete all reps one side before switching.',.
lateral-step-up.why: The lateral step-up trains the glute med and hip abductors through a vertical range in a single-leg lateral loading pattern — the exact demand of the support phase during a skating stride. Standing to the side of the box and stepping up laterally creates a hip abductor drive that bilateral or forward step-ups cannot replicate. It is a fundamental building block in all hockey strength programs.
lateral-step-up.transfer: Trains lateral hip strength — mirrors the side push of skating. Three sets × 8 per leg, controlled. If you push off the down-foot, you cheated. Front foot only.
lateral-step-up.cues: "Step up sideways onto box" · "Drive through lateral leg" · "Stand tall" · "Lower slowly"
lateral-step-up.mistakes: Pushing off the floor foot — all power from the box leg. Knee caving inward — drive it outward over the little toe.',. Box too low — knee height or above for real demand. No pause at the top — stand fully upright on each rep.',.
lateral-step-up.progression: Progress: Weighted lateral step-up with dumbbells, then progress to a lateral step-up with knee drive at the top.', | Regress: Step-up to a lower surface (20cm) until single-leg stability is established.',

paused-split-squat-isometric.name: Paused Split Squat (Isometric)
paused-split-squat-isometric.execution: Take a long split-squat stance — front foot flat, back foot on its toe. Lower straight down — back knee descends until 1 inch from the floor. HOLD. Front shin roughly vertical, back leg extended. Tight glutes both sides. Core braced. Hips square (don't twist). Hold until form breaks. Stand. Switch legs. That's one rep per leg.
paused-split-squat-isometric.why: The paused split squat is a unilateral isometric — single-leg loading held in the deepest position. It directly trains the position of a defensive crouch, a goalie's lateral push-off, or absorbing contact when you're caught mid-stride on one leg. Unilateral isometrics expose left-right imbalances ruthlessly (you can't compensate by leaning) — making this one of the best diagnostic AND development tools for hockey-specific lower-body strength.
paused-split-squat-isometric.transfer: Single-leg isometric hold at the bottom of a split squat — the exact pattern of holding a defensive crouch or absorbing contact one-legged. Triphasic isometric phase, unilateral. Useful diagnostic: if one leg shakes 10 seconds earlier than the other, that's the priority side.
paused-split-squat-isometric.cues: "Take a split-squat stance. Lower until back knee hovers 1 inch from floor. HOLD there. Front knee tracks over toes. Tight glutes. Switch legs."
paused-split-squat-isometric.mistakes: Front knee caving inward — same ACL-risk pattern; track it over the second toe. Hips twisting toward the back leg — re-square them; this is the silent test of hip stability. Holding too shallow (back knee 6+ inches off the floor) — the deep position is the whole point. Bouncing in and out — kills the isometric stimulus. Hold STILL.
paused-split-squat-isometric.progression: Progress: Weighted pause split squat — hold dumbbells at sides or a barbell on the back. | Regress: Pause split squat with hand support (light touch on a bench or chair) — same hold, less balance demand.
paused-split-squat-isometric.muscles: Quadriceps, Glutes, Hip stabilizers, Isometric strength

poliquin-step-up-dbs.name: Poliquin Step-Up (DBs)
poliquin-step-up-dbs.execution: Stand facing a step (15-20cm high) with one foot on the step, heel at the edge. The other foot hangs off the back — this is the non-working leg. Lower the hanging heel toward the floor by bending the step knee. Descend until the hanging heel barely touches the floor. Drive back up through the step heel to standing. All reps one leg before switching. Feel it in the inner quad.
poliquin-step-up-dbs.why: The Poliquin step-up (also called the Bulgarian step-up) specifically targets the VMO (vastus medialis oblique) — the teardrop quad muscle that stabilises the knee cap during the skating knee-bend. Charles Poliquin developed it for hockey players specifically. Weak VMO is directly linked to patellar tracking issues and ACL injury. This exercise addresses the VMO in isolation better than any other movement.
poliquin-step-up-dbs.transfer: Directly targets the VMO — prevents knee injuries common in hockey. Three sets × 8 per leg with dumbbells. Slow tempo, full ROM, both legs balanced.
poliquin-step-up-dbs.cues: "Low box" · "Step up on toes" · "Drive through heel" · "Feel inner quad contract"
poliquin-step-up-dbs.mistakes: Step too high — reduces VMO isolation. 15-20cm is the optimal height. Pushing off the hanging foot — all work from the step leg. Not going low enough — the descent must be sufficient to fully load the VMO. Going too fast — slow, controlled movement maximises VMO activation.
poliquin-step-up-dbs.progression: Progress: Add dumbbells or a weight vest as bodyweight becomes easy. | Regress: Terminal knee extension (TKE) with band — even more isolated VMO activation.

single-leg-press.name: Single-Leg Press
single-leg-press.execution: Set up as a standard leg press but place only one foot on the platform. The working foot is centred — mid-height on the platform. Control the descent — 2-3 seconds down to 90° knee bend. Drive through the full foot to press back up. Stop just short of full lock-out. Complete all reps on one leg before switching. Note the load difference between legs — work to close the gap.
single-leg-press.why: The single-leg press isolates each leg independently on the leg press machine, correcting the strength imbalances that develop from years of dominant-side skating mechanics. Research consistently shows hockey players have 10-20% strength differences between legs — a deficit directly linked to asymmetrical injury risk and power leakage in the skating stride. Equal bilateral leg press strength correlates with more symmetrical skating mechanics.
single-leg-press.transfer: Corrects leg imbalances — most hockey players have a stronger push leg. Pair with single-leg RDL for full unilateral lower-body day. Quad + hamstring, both sides, no compensation.
single-leg-press.cues: "One foot centered" · "Lower to 90°" · "Press through heel" · "Full range of motion"
single-leg-press.mistakes: Knee caving inward during the press — drive it outward over the toes. Too much load — single-leg is roughly 60-65% of your bilateral leg press max. Not noting the imbalance — if you never measure it, you never fix it. Locking out the knee explosively — controlled extension only.
single-leg-press.progression: Progress: Progress toward equal loading on both legs — the goal is bilateral symmetry. | Regress: Leg press with one foot slightly lighter on the platform before going fully single-leg.

single-leg-wall-sit.name: Single-Leg Wall Sit
single-leg-wall-sit.execution: Stand with your back flat against a wall, feet about 50 cm out. Slide down until both thighs are parallel to the floor. Brace your core, then lift one foot 1-2 inches off the floor. All the load is now on the planted leg. Keep the thigh parallel — don't let it rise. HOLD. Hips stay level (no dropping toward the lifted side). Stand, recover briefly, repeat on the other leg. That's one rep per leg.
single-leg-wall-sit.why: A standard wall sit is a brutal quad isometric, but it lets the stronger side compensate — most skaters have a noticeable left/right asymmetry from years of pushing off one leg harder than the other, and a bilateral wall sit hides that. Single-leg wall sit forces each leg to hold the entire load on its own, exposing the asymmetry AND building the weak side directly. The 90° quad isometric in this position is the exact muscle quality of holding a deep skating stance on a single edge — pure off-ice transfer to crossover support and tight-turn outside-leg loading.
single-leg-wall-sit.transfer: Unilateral wall-sit progression that exposes the left/right asymmetry every skater develops. Single-leg isometric quad endurance — the muscle quality of holding a deep stance on one edge. If one side is 10+ seconds weaker, that's your priority leg. Train the weak side first while you're freshest.
single-leg-wall-sit.cues: "Wall sit at parallel — thighs flat" · "Knees at 90°. Lift one foot off the floor. Bottom leg holds everything. No hip drop" · "No twisting. HOLD. Switch legs."
single-leg-wall-sit.mistakes: Hips dropping toward the lifted side — kills the unilateral stimulus; squeeze the planted glute to hold them level. Letting the planted thigh rise above parallel as it gets hard — slide back down or end the set. Resting the lifted foot on the planted shin — that's a sneaky cheat; keep it hovering. Going single-leg before the bilateral version is solid — earn a 90s bilateral wall sit first.
single-leg-wall-sit.progression: Progress: Single-leg wall sit holding a kettlebell at the chest — same hold, much more load. | Regress: Bilateral wall sit — earn 60-90s solid before going single-leg.
single-leg-wall-sit.nameHint: Стульчик у стены на одной ноге

skater-squat.name: Skater Squat
skater-squat.execution: Stand on one leg. The other leg extends behind — NOT touching the floor. Hold a small counterweight (2-5kg plate) at chest height for balance. Lower by bending the standing knee and hinging slightly at the hip. The rear leg swings back for counterbalance. Descend until the rear knee nearly touches the floor. Drive through the heel to stand. Complete all reps then switch.
skater-squat.why: The skater squat (rear-foot-free single-leg squat) is arguably the most demanding unilateral lower-body exercise — it requires simultaneous strength, balance, and hip mobility on a single leg with no rear foot assistance. For hockey players it builds the skating-specific single-leg strength and proprioception that transfers directly to powerful, stable stride mechanics. Mastering this correlates strongly with elite single-leg skating power output.
skater-squat.transfer: Single-leg squat that perfectly mimics the skating position. Three sets × 5 per leg. Difficult enough that 5 honest reps is plenty.
skater-squat.cues: "Balance on one leg" · "Swing arms forward as you lower" · "Tap knee to pad" · "Drive up"
skater-squat.mistakes: Falling forward — the counterweight at the chest helps. If still falling, reduce depth. Rear foot touching the floor for support — it must stay elevated. Knee caving inward — drive it out over the toes. Only going half depth — full range builds full-range strength.
skater-squat.progression: Progress: Hold heavier counterweight or add dumbbells at sides as balance and strength improve. | Regress: Bulgarian split squat — rear foot supported, building the pattern before going unsupported.

skater-squat-bottom-hold.name: Skater Squat Bottom Hold
skater-squat-bottom-hold.execution: Stand on one leg, other leg bent slightly behind you (knee toward the floor). Reach both arms forward as a counterweight. Squat down on the standing leg — the back knee descends toward (but doesn't touch) the floor. HOLD at the bottom: back knee 1-3 inches off the floor, front shin vertical or slightly forward. Tight glute, knee tracks over toes, torso tall (don't dive forward). Stand under control. Switch legs. That's one rep per leg.
skater-squat-bottom-hold.why: The skater squat held at the bottom is the closest off-ice match to the loaded edge position of a tight turn or crossover. Both knees and hips sit at the angles a skater's joints actually live in during the hardest skating positions — not the upright 90° of a normal squat, but the deeper, more diagonal angle where the outside leg loads through an edge. Holding this position builds knee stability and quad/glute strength in the SPECIFIC range hockey demands, in a position where most off-ice training never goes. That's what makes it elite-level transfer for skating.
skater-squat-bottom-hold.transfer: Deep single-leg squat held at the bottom — the exact knee/hip angle of tight turns and crossover edge work. Builds stability in the position skaters actually fail in. If the front knee dives inward, regress to bench-supported. Don't grind a bad position to add seconds.
skater-squat-bottom-hold.cues: "Single-leg squat down — back knee hovers just above the floor" · "Arms forward as a counterweight. HOLD. Tight glute" · "Front shin vertical" · "Knee tracks the toes. Switch legs."
skater-squat-bottom-hold.mistakes: Front knee diving inward as it gets hard — regress immediately; that's the ACL injury pattern. Crashing the back knee into the floor — defeats the hold; control the descent and hover. Diving the torso forward to balance — hips/knees stay deep, but chest stays up. Going single-leg before unilateral split squats are clean — build the base first.
skater-squat-bottom-hold.progression: Progress: Weighted skater squat hold — goblet-hold a dumbbell or kettlebell at the chest. | Regress: Bench-supported skater squat hold — light hand on a chair/bench for balance; full hold remains.
skater-squat-bottom-hold.muscles: Quadriceps, Glutes, Hip stabilizers, Knee stability

band-external-rotation.name: Band External Rotation
band-external-rotation.execution: Anchor a band at elbow height. Stand sideways to the anchor. Grip the band with the far hand. Tuck the elbow firmly against your side at 90°. Starting position: hand pointing toward the anchor (internally rotated). Rotate the hand AWAY from the anchor — externally rotating at the shoulder. Hold the fully-rotated position 2 seconds. Squeeze the back of the shoulder. Return slowly to start — 3 seconds. Elbow stays pinned to the side throughout.
band-external-rotation.why: External rotation weakness is the most common shoulder dysfunction in hockey players — years of internal rotation (stick handling, shooting, forward skating posture) create a dramatic imbalance. Weak external rotators are the primary cause of rotator cuff injuries and shoulder impingement. Two sets of band external rotation daily is the cheapest injury insurance a hockey player can buy.
band-external-rotation.transfer: Rotator cuff prehab — prevents the shoulder injuries common from repeated shooting. External rotation work is non-negotiable for any throwing or pressing athlete. Hockey players push and stick-check — same demand.
band-external-rotation.cues: "Elbow at 90°" · "Rotate arm out" · "Pause at end range" · "Return with control"
band-external-rotation.mistakes: Elbow drifting away from the side — it must stay pinned. Use a towel under the arm if needed. Using momentum or a fast snap — slow and controlled only. Band too heavy — range of motion suffers. Use a light band with full ROM. Only doing it when the shoulder hurts — daily prevention is the entire point.
band-external-rotation.progression: Progress: Side-lying dumbbell external rotation — heavier load, same movement. | Regress: Doorway stretch and isometric external rotation (push hand against a wall) before banding.

barbell-bench-press.name: Barbell Bench Press
barbell-bench-press.execution: Lie on the bench, eyes directly under the bar. Feet flat on floor. Grip slightly wider than shoulders. Wrists straight, NOT bent back. Set the upper back: pinch shoulder blades together and press them DOWN into the bench. Unrack with arms straight. Bring the bar over your sternum. Lower under control — about 2 seconds — to lower chest (nipple line). Bar touches lightly. Press up and slightly back, finishing over the shoulders. Lock out without flaring elbows. Keep the upper back tight for the entire set. Foot drive helps.
barbell-bench-press.why: The bench press develops upper-body pressing strength — vital for protecting yourself in board contact, fending off defenders, and shot power transfer. NHL combine: top prospects bench 1.0-1.2× bodyweight. Hockey players need a balanced press-to-pull ratio (1:1) to avoid the chronic shoulder issues common with pressing-heavy programs.
barbell-bench-press.transfer: Raw upper body pressing strength for checking and battle play. Three sets × 5-6 reps heavy on strength days. Five-rep sets are the sweet spot for hockey-specific pressing strength.
barbell-bench-press.cues: "Arch back" · "Feet flat" · "Lower bar to lower chest" · "Drive up and slightly back"
barbell-bench-press.mistakes: Flaring elbows 90° — shreds the shoulders. Keep elbows ~45-60° from torso. Bouncing the bar off the chest — converts a strength rep into a momentum-fueled cheat. Lifting glutes off the bench — disqualifies the rep in any context that matters. Bar drifting toward the throat — should stay over the chest at the bottom.
barbell-bench-press.progression: Progress: Pause bench (1-2 sec on chest) builds bottom-end strength — direct transfer to checking off the boards. | Regress: Dumbbell bench press first — easier on shoulders, builds pattern with more freedom of movement.

dead-hang.name: Dead Hang
dead-hang.execution: Jump up and grip the pull-up bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Let your body hang completely — arms straight, feet off the floor. Allow the shoulders to shrug up slightly (passive hang) — feel the spine decompress. Relax the entire body. Breathe steadily. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card. Build up over weeks. If grip fails early, use chalk or straps to extend the set.
dead-hang.why: The dead hang decompresses the entire spinal column, counteracting the compressive forces of skating, lifting, and checking. It also builds grip strength and shoulder mobility — hanging from a bar with full shoulder elevation restores the overhead range chronically restricted by hockey posture. NHL medical staff recommend 60-second dead hangs daily as shoulder health maintenance for all positions.
dead-hang.transfer: Builds the grip and shoulder endurance needed before pull-ups become possible — also decompresses the spine. If you can dead-hang 60 seconds at bodyweight, you've earned grip work. If you can't, that's the homework.
dead-hang.cues: "Pronated grip" · "Arms fully extended" · "Shoulders engaged (not shrugged up to ears)" · "Brace core" · "Breathe"
dead-hang.mistakes: Actively pulling the shoulders down — the passive hang (shoulders elevated) decompresses the spine more effectively. Not doing it long enough — under 30 seconds provides minimal benefit. Swinging — stay still and control the hang. Skipping it because it's 'just hanging' — spinal decompression is serious recovery work.
dead-hang.progression: Progress: Single-arm dead hang — massively increases grip and shoulder demand. | Regress: Assisted hang (feet lightly touching the floor) — reduce load while building shoulder comfort.

dumbbell-shoulder-press.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
dumbbell-shoulder-press.execution: Sit on a bench with back support, or stand with feet shoulder-width. Hold dumbbells at shoulder height, elbows at about 75° angle (not flared straight out). Press the dumbbells up and slightly toward each other at the top. Fully lock out at the top — arms straight, biceps near the ears. Lower under control — 2-3 seconds down — back to the starting shoulder position. Keep the core braced — don't arch the lower back to push the weight.
dumbbell-shoulder-press.why: Overhead pressing strength protects the shoulder joint during checks and physical play by strengthening the rotator cuff stabilizers under load. The dumbbell version is preferred over barbell for hockey players because independent arm movement allows natural shoulder tracking — reducing the impingement risk associated with fixed-bar overhead pressing on internally-rotated hockey shoulders.
dumbbell-shoulder-press.transfer: Unilateral shoulder strength — corrects left/right imbalances from stick use. Pair with face pulls or band pull-aparts. Press shouldn't outweigh pull. 2:1 push-pull rule, always.
dumbbell-shoulder-press.cues: "DBs at ear height or KBs in the rack position (handles at shoulder" · "Forearms vertical" · "Knuckles up). Press straight overhead" · "Control the descent."
dumbbell-shoulder-press.mistakes: Flaring elbows to 90° — shoulder impingement risk. Bring elbows slightly forward. Arching the lower back aggressively — if this happens the weight is too heavy. Not reaching full lockout — you're leaving overhead mobility and shoulder health on the table. Rushing the eccentric — the lowering phase builds shoulder stability.
dumbbell-shoulder-press.progression: Progress: Standing single-arm dumbbell press — adds massive core anti-lateral flexion demand. | Regress: Seated machine shoulder press — guided path reduces stabilization demand for beginners.

incline-push-up.name: Incline Push-Up
incline-push-up.execution: Place both hands on a bench, wall, or bar at chest height. The higher the surface, the easier. Walk feet back until the body forms a straight line — ankles to shoulders. Brace the core hard — no sagging hips. Lower the chest toward the surface, elbows at 45° from the torso. Touch the surface with the chest. Press back to full arm extension. Keep the body rigid throughout — don't let the hips pike or sag.
incline-push-up.why: The incline push-up trains upper-body pressing strength with less absolute load than a standard push-up — making it the entry point for players who cannot yet perform quality flat push-ups. The incline shifts the load more toward the upper chest and shoulders. Despite being a beginner tool it is also used by advanced athletes for high-rep shoulder health work and pre-game activation.
incline-push-up.transfer: Beginner pressing variation — builds shoulder stability and chest strength. Three sets × 12-15. Use this as your push-up grease-the-groove drill. Frequency beats intensity for bodyweight strength.
incline-push-up.cues: "Hands on bench" · "Body plank" · "Lower chest toward bench" · "Full extension"
incline-push-up.mistakes: Hips sagging — maintain a straight body line from ankles to shoulders. Elbows flaring to 90° — keep them at 45° to protect the shoulder. Head dropping forward — neutral neck, eyes looking slightly ahead of the hands. Short range of motion — chest must touch the surface and arms must fully extend.
incline-push-up.progression: Progress: Standard push-up — reduce the incline progressively until you reach floor level. | Regress: Wall push-up — highest incline, minimal load. Entry point for complete beginners.

overhead-press.name: Overhead Press
overhead-press.execution: Hold a barbell or dumbbells at shoulder height, elbows slightly in front of the bar. Feet shoulder-width. Core braced hard — do NOT arch the lower back. Press the bar straight up — head moves slightly back to clear the bar path. Once the bar passes the forehead, head moves back under and bar travels in a straight line. Lock out fully at the top — biceps near the ears. Lower under control — 2-3 seconds — back to shoulders.
overhead-press.why: The overhead press builds the shoulder, upper trap, and tricep strength required for physical dominance in the corners and along the boards. For hockey players it also trains the core anti-extension under a vertically-loaded spine — the same bracing pattern needed during contact. Pressing strength overhead directly correlates with the ability to win puck battles when both players are fighting with their arms elevated.
overhead-press.transfer: Builds shoulder stability and overhead strength — important for physical play. Heavy overhead press = a healthy shoulder ten years from now. Skip it at your peril.
overhead-press.cues: "Bar at clavicle" · "Press overhead to lockout" · "Squeeze glutes to protect spine"
overhead-press.mistakes: Excessive lower back arch — if the back arches severely, the weight is too heavy. Bar path drifting forward — bar should travel in a straight vertical line. Not locking out at the top — full overhead range is what keeps shoulders healthy. Flaring elbows wide at the bottom — keep them slightly forward of the bar.
overhead-press.progression: Progress: Single-arm dumbbell press standing — adds massive core anti-lateral flexion demand. | Regress: Seated dumbbell press — back support reduces core demand for beginners.

plate-pinch.name: Plate Pinch
plate-pinch.execution: Hold two 10kg (or two 5kg) plates together with one hand — smooth sides facing out. Pinch the top edge with the fingers on one side and thumb on the other. Hold at your side — do not rest it on your leg. Hold as long as possible. Time it. Switch hands. Rest 90s between attempts. Build hold time progressively each week.
plate-pinch.why: Plate pinching (gripping weight plates between the fingers and thumb) develops the finger flexor strength and pinch grip that directly translates to stick handling under defensive pressure. When a defender cross-checks your hands or you're fighting for a loose puck, pinch grip is what keeps the stick in your hands. Many elite forwards specifically credit grip training for improving their puck-protection ability.
plate-pinch.transfer: Pinch grip strength = stick control + faceoff wins + holding the lane. Direct transfer to gameplay. Pair with farmer carries + wrist roller. Crush grip + carry grip + pinch grip = bulletproof hands.
plate-pinch.cues: "Pinch 2 plates together (smooth side out). Hold for time. No straps. Squeeze hard the entire hold."
plate-pinch.mistakes: Using the palm — pinch grip only. The palm should barely touch the plate. Resting the plate on the thigh — defeats the purpose. Arm hanging straight. Too heavy too soon — build the connective tissue gradually. Skipping the non-dominant hand — both hands equally important.
plate-pinch.progression: Progress: Heavier plates or three-plate pinch — progressively more challenging. | Regress: Towel hang from a pull-up bar — grip strength with a different texture demand.

push-up-challenge-60s.name: Push-Up Challenge (60s)
push-up-challenge-60s.execution: Set a 60-second timer. Get into perfect push-up position. Begin. Pace yourself — go hard but not so hard you blow up in 15 seconds. Every rep must be full ROM: chest to floor, full lockout at top. When form breaks, REST for 2-3 seconds, then continue. Form is non-negotiable. When the timer hits zero, count only the perfect reps. Write it down. That's your baseline.
push-up-challenge-60s.why: Max-rep push-ups in a fixed time window is a classic relative-strength benchmark — it measures how much pressing capacity you can express against your own bodyweight. Hockey demands both strength AND strength endurance: you need to win a battle in the first minute, but you also need to win one in the third period of OT. Tracking this number weekly is one of the simplest, most honest measures of whether your off-ice work is paying off.
push-up-challenge-60s.transfer: Game format = max effort, but FORM FIRST. Beat your previous score. Builds upper-body strength endurance + competitive grit. Track it weekly. Strength endurance is what separates a guy who wins one battle from a guy who wins them all night.
push-up-challenge-60s.cues: "Set a 60-second timer. Do as many push-ups as you can with PERFECT FORM (straight line" · "Chest to floor" · "Full lockout). When form breaks" · "Rest briefly" · "Then continue. Write down the number. Beat it next time."
push-up-challenge-60s.mistakes: Counting half-reps to inflate the number — you're only fooling yourself. Going to absolute failure in 10 seconds, then doing nothing for 50 — pace matters. Skipping the form check — sagging hips, flared elbows, partial range. All disqualifying. Testing this when fatigued — retest only when fresh; otherwise the data is meaningless.
push-up-challenge-60s.progression: Progress: Weighted push-up challenge — add a 5-10 kg vest, same 60-second target. | Regress: Incline push-up challenge — hands on a bench, otherwise identical protocol.

push-up-hold-isometric.name: Push-Up Hold (Isometric)
push-up-hold-isometric.execution: Get into a push-up start position — straight line from heels to head. Lower halfway down — elbows at roughly 90°, chest 4-6 inches off the floor. HOLD. This is the working position. Brace the core, squeeze the glutes, breathe in shallow but steady patterns. Hold until you can no longer maintain a perfect straight line — that's your rep.
push-up-hold-isometric.why: The isometric push-up hold is the 'brace' phase of triphasic upper-body training — and it directly mirrors the position you hold every time you absorb a check, fight for net-front position, or push back on a defender along the boards. Isometric work at long muscle lengths (which is what a half-rep hold is) increases tendon stiffness and improves the rate at which you can express force — the missing link between max strength and on-ice power.
push-up-hold-isometric.transfer: Triphasic isometric phase for upper-body pushing. Hold the bottom of a push-up — builds the "brace" that lets you absorb contact, push off the boards, hold position in front of the net. Useful for absorbing a check, holding net-front position, fighting off a stick lift. The static brace IS the work.
push-up-hold-isometric.cues: "Push-up start. Lower halfway down (elbows ~90°). HOLD. Tight core" · "Straight line head-to-heels. Breathe steadily. Don't sag."
push-up-hold-isometric.mistakes: Holding too high (elbows barely bent) — the 90° position is where the muscle is most challenged. Sagging hips — you're shifting load away from the chest to the lower back. Stop the rep. Holding breath — drops blood pressure, makes the hold less productive. Adding reps when you should be adding time — this is a TIME exercise, not a count.
push-up-hold-isometric.progression: Progress: Single-arm push-up hold (50/50 weight) — doubles the load per arm. | Regress: Incline push-up hold (hands on a bench) — same isometric stimulus, less bodyweight load.
push-up-hold-isometric.muscles: Chest, Triceps, Shoulders, Core, Isometric strength

tricep-dip.name: Tricep Dip
tricep-dip.execution: Grip parallel bars or the edge of a bench, hands at hip width. Straight arms, body vertical — begin the descent. Lower by bending the elbows — go until the upper arms are at least parallel to the floor. Elbows stay close to the body — don't flare wide. Press back to full extension. Pause at the top. Lean slightly forward to shift load to the chest; stay upright for tricep emphasis.
tricep-dip.why: Tricep dips build the elbow extension strength critical for stick separation, pushing opponents off the puck, and the follow-through of a wrist shot. Unlike isolation exercises, dips also load the anterior deltoid and lower pec under full bodyweight, making them a compound upper-body exercise. Hockey players who can perform 15+ strict dips have the tricep and shoulder strength to dominate physical play above the waist.
tricep-dip.transfer: Builds tricep pushing strength — contributes to shot power. Tricep dips are honest. Most athletes can't do 10 with perfect form. Where are you?
tricep-dip.cues: "Hands on bench" · "Lower body" · "Elbows track back" · "Press back to start"
tricep-dip.mistakes: Elbows flaring wide — shoulder impingement risk. Keep them tracking straight back. Half-reps — upper arm must reach parallel to count. Leaning too far forward — turns it into a chest dip. Stay relatively upright for triceps. Locking out with a jerk — controlled full extension.
tricep-dip.progression: Progress: Weighted dip (belt with plates) — adding 10-20kg is a significant milestone. | Regress: Bench dip with feet on floor — reduces load significantly for beginners.

wall-slide.name: Wall Slide
wall-slide.execution: Stand facing a wall. Place both forearms on the wall at shoulder height — elbows bent 90°. Forearms, wrists, and hands all in contact with the wall. Slowly slide both arms UP the wall — straightening the elbows overhead. Keep forearms, wrists, and hands in contact with the wall throughout the slide. Slide as high as possible without the lower back arching or the forearms losing contact. Slide back down. That is one rep. 10-12 reps per set.
wall-slide.why: The wall slide trains the serratus anterior and lower trapezius to control the shoulder blade through a full overhead arc — the exact movement pattern that breaks down in hockey players with impingement. By sliding the forearms up a wall, you train the scapula to upwardly rotate properly overhead, preventing the shoulder blade from pinching the rotator cuff. This is prescribed by virtually every shoulder rehabilitation specialist working with overhead and contact athletes.
wall-slide.transfer: Improves scapular control and overhead shoulder stability. Add wall slides to your warm-up forever. The drill is in the position, not the load.
wall-slide.cues: "Back against wall" · "Press forearms to wall" · "Slide arms up maintaining contact"
wall-slide.mistakes: Arching the lower back to reach higher — brace the core and stay upright. Forearms losing wall contact — if they peel off, you've reached your current limit. Shrugging the traps — keep shoulders DOWN as the arms rise. Going too fast — slow, deliberate slides allow you to feel the scapular movement.
wall-slide.progression: Progress: Band wall slide — add a light band around the wrists for external rotation demand. | Regress: Scapular pull-up — same lower trap activation without the overhead demand.
wall-slide.muscles: Serratus Anterior, Lower Traps, Shoulder Stabilizers

band-assisted-pull-up.name: Band-Assisted Pull-Up
band-assisted-pull-up.execution: Loop a resistance band over the pull-up bar. Step or kneel in the band. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulders, palms forward. Let yourself hang fully — arms straight, shoulders DOWN (not shrugged). Initiate by depressing the shoulder blades, then drive elbows toward your hips. Pull until your chin clears the bar. Pause briefly. Lower under control to a full dead hang. The band assists the hardest range.
band-assisted-pull-up.why: The band-assisted pull-up lets athletes build pull-up strength progressively when they cannot yet complete full bodyweight reps. Building back and grip strength is non-negotiable for hockey — every board battle and puck-protection scenario demands it. The band reduces load at the bottom (hardest point) and teaches the lat engagement pattern needed for strict pull-ups.
band-assisted-pull-up.transfer: Reduces effective bodyweight so you can perform real concentric pull-up reps — the only way to build the pattern. Faster route to a strict pull-up than lat pulldowns alone. The bar position transfers; the cable doesn't.
band-assisted-pull-up.cues: "Loop heavy band over bar" · "Foot in band. Full ROM — chest to bar" · "Full extension at bottom. Lower for 2 seconds."
band-assisted-pull-up.mistakes: Using a band so thick you barely feel any load — challenge yourself. Half-reps — chin must clear the bar AND arms must reach full extension at the bottom. Shrugging at the start instead of depressing the scapulae. Staying on the band too long — test unassisted reps every 2-3 weeks.
band-assisted-pull-up.progression: Progress: Negative pull-ups (jump to chin-over-bar, lower for 5 seconds) before going unassisted. | Regress: Ring row or TRX row — horizontal pull that builds the same muscles with less demand.

barbell-bent-over-row.name: Barbell Bent-Over Row
barbell-bent-over-row.execution: Load a barbell. Stand with feet hip-width, toes under the bar. Hinge at the hips (30-45° torso angle), grip the bar slightly wider than shoulders. Set the back flat — same position as the top of a deadlift. Brace the core hard. Pull the bar toward your lower rib cage by driving elbows BACK. Bar should touch the lower chest/upper abdomen — not the belly button. Lower the bar under control. Don't let it crash or pull your upper back into flexion.
barbell-bent-over-row.why: The barbell row builds the thick upper-back musculature — lats, rhomboids, mid-traps — that wins every puck battle along the boards. It's also the primary counterbalance to bench pressing: for every set of bench you do, you should match it with rowing volume. NHL defensemen who can barbell row 1.5× bodyweight consistently dominate puck battles and rarely suffer shoulder injuries.
barbell-bent-over-row.transfer: Heavy compound pulling — builds the back strength to dominate physical play. Pendlay variant (bar resets on floor each rep) removes the eccentric and lets you go heavier. Choose based on goal.
barbell-bent-over-row.cues: "Hinge to 45°" · "Pull bar to lower chest" · "Squeeze shoulder blades" · "Lower slow"
barbell-bent-over-row.mistakes: Using the lower back to heave the bar up — this is a ROW, not a deadlift. Torso stays still. Pulling toward the belly button — pulls to the lower chest for full lat engagement. Rounding the upper back — set it before pulling, keep it set throughout. Using straps before your grip deserves them — build grip strength naturally first.
barbell-bent-over-row.progression: Progress: Pendlay row (dead stop from the floor each rep) — eliminates momentum and demands more power. | Regress: Dumbbell row — easier to learn the hinge position with one arm at a time.

barbell-bicep-curl.name: Barbell Bicep Curl
barbell-bicep-curl.execution: Stand holding dumbbells at your sides, palms facing forward. Keeping elbows pinned to your sides, curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders. Squeeze the biceps hard at the top. Lower under control — 2-3 seconds down. The eccentric builds more strength than the curl up. Full extension at the bottom — don't cut the range short. Alternate arms or curl together — both work.
barbell-bicep-curl.why: Forearm and bicep strength matter more in hockey than most players realize — your grip on the stick is what connects all your skating power to the puck. Strong biceps also help decelerate the arm during shooting (protecting the elbow) and contribute to the pulling mechanics in board battles. Not vanity — function.
barbell-bicep-curl.transfer: Builds elbow flexor strength for stick lifting and board battles. Pair with tricep work — bicep alone = imbalance. Both flex AND extension at the elbow get loaded.
barbell-bicep-curl.cues: "Elbows fixed at sides" · "Curl to chin" · "Squeeze at top" · "Slow 3-second descent"
barbell-bicep-curl.mistakes: Swinging the torso — if you need momentum, the weight is too heavy. Letting elbows drift forward — pin them to your sides. Partial reps — full range, every rep. Rushing the eccentric — the slow lowering is WHERE the gains happen.
barbell-bicep-curl.progression: Progress: Zottman curl (curl up with palms up, rotate to palms DOWN and lower slowly) — trains both biceps and forearm extensors. | Regress: Resistance band curl — lighter and easier to control for beginners.

chest-supported-dumbbell-row.name: Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row
chest-supported-dumbbell-row.execution: Set an adjustable bench to 30-45° incline. Lie face-down on the bench, chest supported, feet on the floor or footrest. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down. Row both dumbbells up toward your hips, leading with the elbows. Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top for a 1-second hold. Lower with control — 2-3 seconds — until arms are fully extended. No bouncing.
chest-supported-dumbbell-row.why: The chest-supported row eliminates lower-back fatigue from rowing — you lie face-down on an incline bench, so the bench holds your spine in place while your back muscles do all the work. For hockey players, that's huge: every other rowing variation also taxes the spinal erectors, which are already getting hammered by squats, deadlifts, and just the act of skating in a forward-flexed posture. This row gives you all the upper-back stimulus with none of the back fatigue.
chest-supported-dumbbell-row.transfer: Eliminates lower back fatigue — lets you focus purely on back strength. Three sets × 10-12. Heavy enough that the last rep is honest. The bench is your insurance policy — use it.
chest-supported-dumbbell-row.cues: "Lie prone on incline bench" · "Pull dumbbells to sides" · "Squeeze shoulder blades"
chest-supported-dumbbell-row.mistakes: Lifting the chest off the bench to cheat the weight up — defeats the entire point. Rowing the dumbbells too high (to the armpits) — over-recruits the upper traps instead of the mid-back. Going too heavy — when form breaks, the lower back kicks in to compensate. Lose the weight. Skipping the squeeze at the top — the peak contraction is where the rhomboids fire hardest.
chest-supported-dumbbell-row.progression: Progress: Single-arm chest-supported row — anti-rotation challenge added; more shoulder-blade ROM. | Regress: Bench-supported dumbbell row (one hand on bench, knee on bench) — easier setup, similar pattern.

chin-up.name: Chin-Up
chin-up.execution: Grip the bar shoulder-width, palms facing toward you (supinated). Dead hang — arms fully extended, shoulders pulled down away from ears. Initiate by squeezing the shoulder blades down and together. Pull elbows toward your hips — chin rises toward and then above the bar. Pause 1 second at the top with chin clearly over the bar. Lower under complete control for 2-3 seconds back to full hang.
chin-up.why: The chin-up (palms facing you) recruits more bicep contribution than a pull-up, making it the superior upper-body builder for overall pulling strength. For hockey players it develops the same lat/mid-back chain as the pull-up while also adding the forearm and elbow flexor strength that controls a stick in traffic. A strong chin-up also protects the shoulder by keeping the posterior capsule healthy through full overhead range.
chin-up.transfer: Supinated grip activates more bicep — great for puck protection strength. Pair with horizontal row on the same day for full back-pattern coverage. Vertical + horizontal pull = bulletproof shoulders.
chin-up.cues: "Underhand grip" · "Pull chest to bar" · "Squeeze lats and biceps at top"
chin-up.mistakes: Kipping or swinging — zero value. Strict reps only. Stopping short of full arm extension at the bottom — you need the full stretch. Letting the elbows flare wide — keep them tracking close to the body. Going too fast on the way down — the eccentric builds the most strength.
chin-up.progression: Progress: Weighted chin-up with a dip belt — adding 10 kg is a major strength milestone. | Regress: Band-assisted chin-up or negative chin-up (jump to top, lower for 5 seconds).

dumbbell-row.name: Dumbbell Row
dumbbell-row.execution: Place one hand and same-side knee on a bench. Other foot on the floor wide for stability. Grip the dumbbell with the free hand — arm hanging straight below the shoulder. Set the back flat and parallel to the floor. Pull the dumbbell toward your hip — elbow drives back and up. At the top, squeeze the lat hard. Pause 1 second. Lower the dumbbell all the way to full arm extension. Complete stretch at the bottom.
dumbbell-row.why: The single-arm dumbbell row trains unilateral back strength while requiring the core to resist rotation — a direct hockey transfer. When you pull an opponent off the puck, pin someone to the boards, or recover your stick in a battle, this exact unilateral pulling pattern is what does the work. The greater range of motion vs. barbell rows also allows better lat stretch and contraction.
dumbbell-row.transfer: Back thickness and pulling power — crucial for board battles. 2 pull sets for every push set. Dumbbell rows are easy volume to hit that ratio.
dumbbell-row.cues: "One hand on bench" · "Pull dumbbell to hip" · "Elbow close to body" · "Squeeze at top"
dumbbell-row.mistakes: Rotating the torso to heave the weight — the back stays parallel to the floor throughout. Pulling toward the chest instead of the hip — lat engagement requires pulling toward the hip. Short range of motion — full extension at the bottom, full contraction at the top. Using too heavy a weight — form degrades to torso rotation. Drop the weight.
dumbbell-row.progression: Progress: Chest-supported dumbbell row (lie on incline bench) — removes all torso momentum. | Regress: Band row standing — same unilateral pull with easier load management.

hammer-curl.name: Hammer Curl
hammer-curl.execution: Stand holding dumbbells at sides, palms facing each other (neutral grip). Pin the elbows to your sides — they must not drift forward. Curl both dumbbells toward your shoulders in a smooth arc. Thumbs should be pointing toward the shoulders at the top. Squeeze at the top. Lower for 2-3 seconds — full extension at the bottom. Alternate arms or curl together — both work.
hammer-curl.why: The hammer curl (neutral grip, thumbs up) trains the brachioradialis and brachialis — the muscles that give real elbow flexor strength for stick handling under defensive pressure. More importantly it builds forearm girth and wrist stability, which directly translates to shot power transfer and one-hand stick control. Most hockey players have significantly underdeveloped forearms relative to the demands placed on them.
hammer-curl.transfer: Neutral grip builds brachialis — increases overall elbow strength for checking. Pair with wrist roller for a complete forearm + grip session. Quiet day, high payoff.
hammer-curl.cues: "Neutral grip (thumbs up)" · "Curl to shoulder height" · "Squeeze" · "Lower slow"
hammer-curl.mistakes: Swinging the torso — if you're swinging, the weight is too heavy. Elbows drifting forward — the upper arm must stay vertical. Rushing the lowering phase — the 2-3 second eccentric builds the brachialis strength. Neglecting this for 'real' exercises — forearm strength has direct game impact.
hammer-curl.progression: Progress: Cross-body hammer curl (curl across the body toward the opposite shoulder) — more brachialis engagement. | Regress: Band hammer curl — lighter load, easier to maintain form.

inverted-row.name: Inverted Row
inverted-row.execution: Set up a bar or sturdy table at hip height. Lie underneath, grab the bar with hands shoulder-width or slightly wider, palms facing away. Body straight from heels to head — same plank rigidity as a push-up. Pull the chest to the bar by squeezing the shoulder blades down and back. Pause at the top — chest touches the bar. Lower with control to arms fully extended. That's one rep.
inverted-row.why: The inverted row is the bodyweight horizontal pull — the row equivalent of a push-up. It builds the upper-back strength (rhomboids, mid-traps, rear delts, lats, biceps) that protects the shoulders from the cumulative damage of a hockey season. Players who can do 10+ strict inverted rows have measurably better posture, fewer shoulder issues, and stronger stick-checks. It's also the single best stepping stone to the pull-up if you can't do one yet.
inverted-row.transfer: Bodyweight horizontal pull — builds the upper-back strength that protects shoulders and powers stick-checks. The pull-up's easier cousin. 2:1 pull-push ratio: for every push set, two pull sets. Inverted rows are how you hit that without equipment.
inverted-row.cues: "Lie under a bar or sturdy table. Grab overhead" · "Body straight from heels to head. Pull chest to bar. Lower with control. Squeeze shoulder blades at the top."
inverted-row.mistakes: Hips sagging — defeats the row by letting the body drop instead of pulling up. Pulling with the arms only — initiate with the shoulder blades, finish with the arms. Half-reps (chest never reaches the bar) — full ROM only counts. Setting the bar too low so it becomes too hard — work up gradually; the lower the bar, the harder the row.
inverted-row.progression: Progress: Weighted inverted row (plate on chest) once you hit 15 strict reps · or bar 1 set lower (closer to ground = harder). | Regress: Set the bar higher (waist or chest height) — same movement, less of your bodyweight is loaded.

lat-pulldown.name: Lat Pulldown
lat-pulldown.execution: Sit at the pulldown machine, thighs secured under the pad. Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width. Lean back slightly — about 10-15°. This is not a row; maintain this angle throughout. Pull the bar down to upper chest level — elbows drive DOWN and BACK. Squeeze the lats at full contraction. Pause 1 second. Return under full control — arms extend to full hang at the top. Feel the stretch. Do not let the stack clang — control the weight the entire rep.
lat-pulldown.why: The lat pulldown builds the same pulling muscles as the pull-up — lats, rhomboids, biceps, rear delts — but with adjustable load making it accessible for all strength levels. For hockey players building from zero pull-up capacity, the lat pulldown is the primary back strength builder. Strong lats are critical for powerful checking, stick handling under pressure, and the overhead reach required for physical play.
lat-pulldown.transfer: Builds lat strength — critical for stick handling and shot follow-through. Lat pulldown is supplemental to pull-ups, not a replacement. Pull-ups first; pulldowns when you need more volume.
lat-pulldown.cues: "Lean slightly back" · "Pull bar to upper chest" · "Squeeze lats" · "Slow return"
lat-pulldown.mistakes: Pulling behind the neck — cervical spine compression risk. Always pull to the front. Using momentum to heave the bar — the torso angle should remain constant. Not reaching full arm extension at the top — the stretch at the top is where you build range. Grip too wide — very wide grip actually reduces lat range of motion.
lat-pulldown.progression: Progress: Weighted pull-up — unassisted bodyweight replaces the machine as strength builds. | Regress: Band-assisted pull-up or ring row — lighter load alternatives.',

pull-up.name: Pull-Up
pull-up.execution: Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulders, palms forward (overhand). Hang from a dead position — arms fully extended, shoulders pulled DOWN AND BACK (no shrug). Initiate by depressing the shoulder blades, then pull the elbows down toward your hips. Pull until your chin clears the bar. Pause briefly. Lower under control to a full dead hang. NO half-reps. Reset shoulder position before next rep.
pull-up.why: Pull-ups train the lats, mid-back, and grip — the entire upper-body chain that wins board battles and protects the puck. NHL combine standard: forwards 12+, defensemen 14+ strict pull-ups. Strong pulls also balance pressing volume (bench, OHP), preventing the rounded-shoulder posture that wrecks shoulder health over a season.
pull-up.transfer: Builds the pulling strength needed for board battles and stick control. Weighted pull-ups at 1.5× bodyweight = elite hockey benchmark. Aim there. The road is decades long; start today.
pull-up.cues: "Dead hang start" · "Drive elbows to pockets" · "Chin over bar" · "Lower with control"
pull-up.mistakes: Kipping (using leg swing) — counts as 0 strict reps. Looks like you're stronger than you are. Half-reps — never reaching chin to bar OR never returning to full dead hang. Shrugging up at the start — kills lat engagement. Lock shoulders DOWN before pulling. Flaring elbows wide — less efficient than driving them toward your hips.
pull-up.progression: Progress: Weighted pull-ups (belt + plate). Adding 25 lbs is roughly the size of one full bodyweight rep. | Regress: Negative pull-ups (jump up, lower for 5s). Build eccentric strength first. Once you can hang for 30s, target 1 strict rep.

ring-row-inverted-row.name: Ring Row / Inverted Row
ring-row-inverted-row.execution: Set rings or TRX straps at about waist height. Grip the handles, lean back with arms extended — heels on the floor. Body is in a straight line from heels to head — like a reverse plank. Pull the handles to your lower chest — elbows drive back and outward. Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top. Pause 1 second. Lower under control back to full arm extension.
ring-row-inverted-row.why: The ring row (or TRX row) is the horizontal pull that builds back strength in athletes who cannot yet do pull-ups. By adjusting body angle, you can scale load from very easy (upright) to very hard (body parallel to the floor). For hockey players it builds the same lat/mid-back/bicep strength as the pull-up with lower absolute demand — making it the perfect gateway exercise to vertical pulling.
ring-row-inverted-row.transfer: Bodyweight horizontal pull — builds the back strength needed before vertical pulling. Rings are the most underutilized tool for shoulder-friendly pulling work. Use them.
ring-row-inverted-row.cues: "Set bar/rings at hip height" · "Body straight" · "Pull chest to bar" · "Pause 1 sec" · "Lower controlled"
ring-row-inverted-row.mistakes: Hips sagging — rigid body line throughout. Squeeze glutes. Pulling to the belly instead of the lower chest. Too upright (easy) — walk the feet forward to increase the angle and load. Shrugging the traps instead of retracting the shoulder blades.
ring-row-inverted-row.progression: Progress: Feet elevated ring row (body below horizontal) — approaches the difficulty of a pull-up. | Regress: More upright body angle — walk feet back until the movement is achievable with good form.

scapular-pull-up.name: Scapular Pull-Up
scapular-pull-up.execution: Hang from a pull-up bar in a dead hang — arms straight, body relaxed. Without bending the elbows, pull the shoulder blades DOWN and TOGETHER. Your body will rise slightly (2-5cm) — this is the scapular depression. Hold at the top for 2-3 seconds. Feel the lower traps fire. Lower back to a passive hang. Repeat. 10 reps per set — quality of contraction matters more than speed.
scapular-pull-up.why: The scapular pull-up (dead hang with shoulder blade depression) isolates the lower trapezius and serratus anterior — the muscles that control scapular position and protect the rotator cuff during all overhead and pulling activities. Hockey players with poor scapular control develop chronic shoulder impingement and rotator cuff issues. This simple drill done daily is foundational shoulder health work.
scapular-pull-up.transfer: Trains the FIRST inch of a pull-up — scapular depression — which is what most beginners are weak in. Pair with band-assisted pull-ups for progressive pull-up build. Both essential, neither sufficient alone.
scapular-pull-up.cues: "Hang from bar" · "Arms straight. Pull shoulder blades DOWN and BACK without bending elbows. 1 second pause."
scapular-pull-up.mistakes: Bending the elbows — this becomes a pull-up. Straight arms only. Shrugging instead of depressing — the blade moves DOWN, not up. Only using it as a warm-up — it's also valuable as a standalone exercise. Rushing through the reps — the 2-3 second hold is where the lower trap fires.
scapular-pull-up.progression: Progress: Add a slight lean back and hold with more shoulder blade compression — increases demand. | Regress: Band pull-apart — same lower trap activation without the hanging demand.

seated-cable-row.name: Seated Cable Row
seated-cable-row.execution: Sit at the cable row station, feet on the platform, knees slightly bent. Grip the handle — narrow (V-grip) for more lat; wide for more rear delt. Sit tall, chest up. Pull the handle to your lower sternum — elbows drive back. Squeeze shoulder blades together at full contraction. Hold 1 second. Extend arms fully under control — feel the stretch in the lats. Don't round the back to reach further — stop where your spine stays neutral.
seated-cable-row.why: The seated cable row builds the horizontal pulling strength that dominates puck battles — the mid-back, lats, and rear delts all working together to control an opponent or protect the puck. Unlike barbell rows, the cable keeps constant tension throughout the full range of motion, making it superior for building the thick mid-back that hockey players need for durability.
seated-cable-row.transfer: Constant tension on back muscles — excellent for mid-back thickness. Cable row is the safest heavy-pull variant for anyone with a cranky lower back. Same lat stimulus, no spine load.
seated-cable-row.cues: "Sit tall" · "Pull handle to belly button" · "Squeeze shoulder blades" · "Slow release"
seated-cable-row.mistakes: Using torso momentum to heave the weight — stay upright, pull with the back. Pulling to the belly button instead of the lower chest — shortens lat engagement. Not reaching full arm extension — the stretch is where you build the range. Shrugging the traps — pull shoulder blades DOWN and BACK, not up.
seated-cable-row.progression: Progress: Single-arm cable row — unilateral loading increases core anti-rotation demand. | Regress: Band row — same movement with less load and no stability requirement.

towel-pull-up-hold.name: Towel Pull-Up Hold
towel-pull-up-hold.execution: Loop two towels over a pull-up bar. Grip one towel in each hand. Perform a pull-up or jump to the chin-over-bar position. Hold at the top for as long as possible — goal is 10-30 seconds. Lower slowly — control the descent against the towel's give. Rest 90 seconds. Repeat 3-4 times. If hanging is too hard, use a slightly supported foot on a box.
towel-pull-up-hold.why: Hanging from a towel looped over a bar trains grip strength in the exact hand position used for stick handling — fingers wrapped around a cylindrical object under tension. The isometric hold at chin-over-bar level builds the forearm flexors, brachialis, and hand muscles simultaneously. This is a favourite grip strength tool of wrestlers and climbers — athletes who, like hockey players, win by out-gripping their opponents.
towel-pull-up-hold.transfer: Thick-grip work using towels = brutal grip endurance. Directly carries over to holding stick through battles and tie-ups. Useful for athletes who can do many pull-ups but want grip-specific overload. Direct hockey carry-over.
towel-pull-up-hold.cues: "Drape 2 towels over bar. Grip the towels (not the bar). Hold for time at top of pull-up."
towel-pull-up-hold.mistakes: Letting the shoulders shrug up — keep them depressed even in the hold. Dropping quickly — control the descent for extra time under tension. Gripping too low on the towel — grip at the top for the most challenging position. Wrists bending backward — keep them neutral throughout.
towel-pull-up-hold.progression: Progress: Single-towel hold (both hands on one towel) — demands more grip concentration. | Regress: Regular dead hang from the bar — build basic grip endurance before the towel.

wrist-roller.name: Wrist Roller
wrist-roller.execution: Hold a wrist roller (or a dowel with a rope and weight attached) with both hands. Arms extended straight in front of you at shoulder height — or hanging down. Roll the weight UP by alternating wrist curls — one hand at a time. Once fully rolled up, slowly unroll by reversing the direction. Keep the arms as steady as possible — only the wrists should move. 3-4 complete roll-ups per set.
wrist-roller.why: The wrist roller builds forearm extensor and flexor endurance simultaneously — rolling the weight up and down trains the entire forearm under sustained load that cannot be replicated by standard curls. For hockey players, forearm endurance directly translates to stick-handling quality in overtime and late in the third period when fatigued forearms produce weaker, less precise shot releases and puck control.
wrist-roller.transfer: Builds forearm and wrist strength — directly improves shot power and stick control. If you've never trained forearms directly, you've been leaving shot velocity on the table. Start.
wrist-roller.cues: "Arms extended" · "Roll weight up with wrists alternating" · "Control the lowering"
wrist-roller.mistakes: Arms dropping — keep them at the target height (shoulder for hardest, waist for easier). Going too fast on the unroll — slow eccentric unrolling builds as much strength as the roll-up. Weight too heavy — should be able to complete 3 full roll-ups without the arms shaking uncontrollably. Skipping it — nothing else builds forearm endurance this comprehensively.
wrist-roller.progression: Progress: Arms extended at shoulder height (hardest) instead of hanging at the waist. | Regress: Less weight — reduce the hanging load until the movement is controlled.
